summary.text: A neuron, or nerve cell, is an electrically excitable cell that communicates with other cells by firing electric signals called action potentials.
Neurons receive and conduct impulses and pass them on through synapses, which commonly use tiny amounts of chemical neurotransmitters.
They form neural networks, mostly in the brain and spinal cord, and are the main components of nervous tissue in all animals except sponges and placozoans.

facts.label: Three types
facts.value: Sensory neurons, motor neurons and interneurons

facts.label: Axon length
facts.value: As far as 1 meter in humans, more in other species

facts.label: Cell body size
facts.value: Varies from 4 to 100 micrometers in diameter

facts.label: Who has none
facts.value: Plants and fungi do not have nerve cells

items.prompt: A neuron takes in messages from its neighbours and then passes its own message onward. Which part carries the outgoing message?
items.explain: Most neurons receive signals through the dendrites and soma and send signals out along the axon.

items.prompt: A neuron's voltage changes by a large enough amount in a short time. What does the neuron do?

options.label: Fires an all-or-nothing pulse that travels along its axon
Fires a pulse sized to match the change
Stores the change until the next day

items.explain: Past the threshold, the neuron generates an all-or-nothing electrochemical pulse called an action potential, which travels rapidly along the axon.

items.prompt: Your fingertip brushes something hot. Which type of neuron responds to the touch and sends signals toward the spinal cord?
items.explain: Sensory neurons respond to stimuli such as touch, sound or light and send signals to the spinal cord and then the brain.

items.prompt: One neuron's only job is to link two other neurons in the same region of the spinal cord. What type is it?
items.explain: Interneurons connect neurons to other neurons within the same region of the brain or spinal cord.

items.prompt: A gardener wonders whether a fern has nerve cells like a squirrel does. What is the answer?

options.label: Yes, but only in its roots
No, plants and fungi lack them
Yes, but they are much smaller
Only when it is growing in light

items.explain: Plants and fungi do not have nerve cells.

items.prompt: Someone hopes to grow lots of brand-new brain neurons in their fifties. According to the usual pattern, when are most neurons made?

options.label: At a steady rate throughout adult life
Mostly in old age to replace worn cells
Only during sleep at any age

items.explain: Neural stem cells generate most neurons during brain development and childhood, and neurogenesis largely stops in adulthood in most brain areas.

paragraphs.heading: A cell that fires
paragraphs.text: A neuron, also spelled neurone or simply called a nerve cell, is a cell that can be excited electrically. It talks to other cells by firing electric signals called action potentials. Neurons link up into networks, mostly in the brain and spinal cord. They are the main building blocks of nervous tissue in every animal except sponges and placozoans, and plants and fungi have none.

paragraphs.heading: Three jobs
paragraphs.text: Neurons are usually sorted into three types by what they do. Sensory neurons react to things like touch, sound or light and pass signals to the spinal cord and on to the brain. Motor neurons take signals from the brain and spinal cord and control everything from muscle contractions to what glands release. Interneurons connect neurons to other neurons in the same part of the brain or spinal cord.

paragraphs.heading: The parts of a neuron
paragraphs.text: A neuron has the usual parts of any cell, such as a nucleus and mitochondria, plus some of its own. The soma, or cell body, is compact. Dendrites branch heavily out of it and reach a few hundred micrometres. The axon starts from a bulge on the soma, the axon hillock, and can run as far as 1 metre in humans, ending in axon terminals that pass the signal on.

paragraphs.heading: How a signal moves
paragraphs.text: Most neurons take in signals through their dendrites and soma and send them out along the axon. Neurons keep a voltage difference across their membrane. If that voltage shifts far enough in a short time, the neuron fires an action potential, an all-or-nothing pulse that races down the axon. When it reaches a synapse, a specialised connection, a tiny amount of a chemical called a neurotransmitter usually carries the signal across the gap to the next cell.

paragraphs.heading: Go or stop
paragraphs.text: Signals arriving at a synapse can be excitatory or inhibitory. Excitatory ones raise the overall voltage reaching the soma, and inhibitory ones lower it. When several neurons are joined so that they work together, they form a neural circuit.

paragraphs.heading: Made early in life
paragraphs.text: Most neurons are produced by neural stem cells while the brain develops and during childhood. In most areas of the adult brain, making new neurons largely stops. Neurons share the nervous system with glial cells, which give them structural and metabolic support.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient invention
paragraphs.text: Molecular evidence suggests living things first became able to produce electric signals some 700 to 800 million years ago. The forerunners of neurons were secretory cells. Over time they picked up new gene modules that let them build ion channels able to make fast electrical signals. That ability was a key step in how the nervous system evolved.
